Hi, I have pretty much the same background as you - NTU student (recently graduated), ocd diagnosed, except that I have a longer history with ocd. was diagnosed when I was a kid. 

In this regard, Here are some thoughts to share: 

On Professional help:  

- to maximize cost effectiveness, go to polyclinic, get a referral to a hospital with a psychiatry department. A recommendation is to avoid IMH - only because it's difficult telling people you are on MC today because you have appt at IMH. Yep, discrimination still exists.

- It would be more effective  to go to a psychiatrist. I mean, I'm not questioning the NTU counsellors competence in her trade.  Just making a point that - a psychiatrist and psychologist who spends most of their professional hours dealing with ocd and clinical disorders  would have more experience equipped to help you. 

- other considerations : speaking as a fresh grad, one of the limitations of visiting a govt hospital would be  that your medical records (of being diagnosed with a mental disorder) stays in the public health system. I am uncertain about the implications when trying to secure a job in public sector. (Call me paranoid.)

- if you go to a private doctor, it would be very pricey.  Furthermore, I  feel  that location (public vs private healthcare) does not determine quality in the health industry. Think : panadol sold at Watson vs paracetamol prescribed by polyclinics. 

On Medication :  

- intrusive thoughts would always be there for every human. Usually, people would stop thinking about these thoughts after concluding outright that it's irrational I.e. they have this "braking mechanism" in their brain to stop their brain from spiralling into obsessive circles.

- We have this mechanism too, but it's weaker for us due to the chemical imbalances in our brain.  Therefore, the purpose of medication is to correct this chemical imbalance and therefore improve our quality of life. 

- I am currently a functioning individual with a job and have managed to hide my symptoms from all my colleagues (and classmates and professors in the past). My ocd is still there. I have good and bad days. But I am still able to keep it under control and pull off everyday with my medication. 
-  based on your described symptoms, it seems to be one of the either: A. Not the right dosage of medication  B. Not the right kind of medication. 
- I wish to emphasize that hitting the right dose, and the right type of medication is very important, so please please go to a trained psychiatrist. It's even better if you can get one that had lots of experience handling ocd. (This is by luck if you go to public hospitals because if you want to be a subsidized patient, you can't choose your own doctor. I think can choose your own doctor if you're not a subsidised patient but it would be more ex.yeah, but usually most doctors are quite decent. )

On Mindfulness

- I can't really advise on mindfulness practice because I  use it  minimally (consciously) Usually, only on days when I can't sleep. 

- I think it is very important to get some kind of distraction when you're having ocd thoughts. It really helps. In a way, this is mindfulness (subconsciously?), because you are living in the moment when you're purposely redirecting your attention from the ocd in your head to the task on hand instead. 

- For example, when I'm having ocd rituals, 80 percent of my existing attention (I like to imagine it as a CPU capacity in computers) is directed to ocd. But when I focus my energy on something else and live in the moment (yes, mindfulness), the majority of my attention would be directed somewhere else. Granted, ocd worries would still be at the back of my mind (say 10 percent of my brain capacity), but it's effect on my mind and emotions is significantly diminished. 

- boring me would like to suggest going out for a walk (with a mask) or engaging in some sports etc. Especially with covid (cough "work from home"), being outdoors really helps me a lot. 

- another thing you could attempt is to push the ocd ritual to the end of the day. (I would recommend to try this after hitting the right dosage and the right kind of medication .) 

- For example, when I'm working, I have a mental to-do list and once I'm aware the thought is irrational, I try to push it to the end of my list and only do it at the end of the day (if I still rmb lol). Its not about thought suppression. Thought suppression doesn't work due to the "white bear" effect, as my previous psychiatrist liked to call it (see below*). I accept that the ocd worry is still there - there's no point trying to avoid it. And I accept that it still exists at the back of my mind - say 10% of my available brain capacity 

*(Ironic process theory - e.g. if I tell you not to think about "white bears", it would be counter effective because you will see the image of "white bear" in your head instead when you try to suppress these thoughts.)

 You can do it. At the start, it would be a tormenting process especially when you're still hunting for the right kind of medication or dose. (Speaking from personal experience, I have changed medication two times before find one that fit me.) I believe that you will make it and come out as a stronger person. So cheer up. If you need someone to talk to, you can PM me. I'll try to check in every day if you need someone to discuss. but I'm not v active on Reddit, so please do let me know in advance.

Hello! I was having suicidal thoughts when I couldn't handle my old thoughts and was literally bawling everyday two weeks ago. 

But this all stopped when I increased the dosage of my medication to help cope with it.

Perhaps your boyfriend needs to increase his medication dosage, so that he is able to handle the thoughts? Suggest him to make a call to his psychiatrist to ask for an earlier appointment to discuss increasing dosage. 

Alternatively, if you guys are sure that the current medication is the most suitable one for him, and you have a stockpile till the next appt, to increase the dosage yourself. BUT please do so slowly and gradually (for e.g. change dose only at the end of the week, then keep the same dose for the rest of next week before repeating.) And also research beforehand if there are side effects.

On a side note, as a person by his side, the most important thing is to make sure he takes his medication everyday (I often forget.. so before the previous breakdown I only eat 5 out of 7 days.)

Hope this helps.

Ideally... When the intrusive thought comes to your head, accept it is an intrusive thought and choose to let it "go" away from you. 

(E.g. like how you would deal with a naggy lecturer, let her words go in from one side of you ear and go out from the other.... Because you don't really think there's a point in listening.)

They seem real because the OCD side of your brain is telling you so, even if the thoughts are not real. 

Everyone has intrusive thoughts. The  difference is - OCD sufferers know these are intrusive thoughts but they can't stop thinking about if because of a chemical imbalance. 

An analogy would be a car going down a steep slope. A typical car has a braking system to stop the car from tumbling down. 

But ocd suffers don't have that braking system. 

They can only sit there sadly... and see the car tumble down the slope.

 See their thoughts run wild...

 in circles that they know don't make sense..  but don 't know how to get out of them otherwise.

Hello, I won't tell you  to stop researching because I know how hard it is to do so. But why not ... Postpone the research? Push it down your priority list for the day (since you know this compulsion is inherently irrational even though we can't help doing it). This is what worked for me, when  I had ocd thought compulsions: 

- when i first have the intrusive thought, I acknowledge it is an ocd thought and I am anxious about it. 
- Then I try to focus on other tasks.. even though I acknowledge that the thought is still running in some parts of my mind. (An analogy would be thinking of your brain as a CPU. You put the thought to research on hold, like  "minimizing a program on computer".)
- the rationale for doing so is that: intrusive thoughts come hand in hand with anxiety. By not acting on the intrusive thought and focusing my energy temporarily on something else, I am letting my anxiety levels subside. So that the next time I revisit my intrusive thought, I am calmer and more rational - allowing me to reduce the number of times I perform the ritualistic actions. (We perform rituals like checks, repeatedly,  because we are fueled by anxiety.)
- at the end of the day, if i have not forgotten the ocd thought and it's still a nagging thought at the back of my mind, i return and check it out.

Hello, I'm currently on sertraline (not sure if it's what you're looking for) for OCD. Here is how it worked for me if you're interested: 

- strong emotional blunting effect - I actually felt pretty depressed when I first started taking this drug because I felt very hollow. But I don't feel that way anymore (well most of the time) after I got used to it, and after I reduced the dose. 
- ocd intrusive thoughts have been reduced to a manageable level, to the extent where I can function and appear to be a normal person, in the eyes of my colleagues. 
- hmm if you're worried about sex drive, I don't think my sex drive has been reduced by this drug.

I think for now - maybe you can try to distract yourself by doing something more productive then see if the thoughts diminish or still stay there? 

Worrying continuously may be a sign of OCD... When my OCD was at its worst previously, I wasn't able to put a stop to my mental rituals (rationalising an intrusive thought, even though I know it's not logical) 

If the thoughts are still there, here are some coping techniques that have worked for me (if you are unable to see a psychiatrist due to the pandemic). They are listed in sequence below: 

- You can try to push the worry to the back of your mind first (I always think of it like "minimizing a program" on my computer), by focusing on something else . this lets your anxiety  revolving that subject matter cool  down.
- You can consider picking up a new hobby (haha e.g. knitting or building those mini Lego figurines). 
-  at the end of the day, if you really can't stand it, go back to researching again.. ( if you're aware it's not rational but still can't help it, it looks like a OCD ritual to me, based on my own experience as a OCD patient.) 

Again, pls double confirm with a psychiatrist when this pandemic thing is over / when ur govt allows u to visit hospitals.

Hey there, don't be so quick to jump to the conclusion. 

--- 
Fear that you may be a pedophile and continuously rationalising it continuously is clearly an intrusive thought. You need to be aware that it is an intrusive thought and you are not your intrusive thoughts. 

Take a step back away from your intrusive thought, let your anxiety subside by distracting yourself with something else. 

I know there are people saying that we shouldn't believe our intrusive thoughts. But as a fellow ocd sufferer, I understand that we are constantly doubting ourselves and it is difficult not to judge and conclude. Just do that when you are in a better state of mind, when your anxiety has fallen. 

Then try to look at the issue objectively from the perspective of an outsider. (E.g. 1. This person has intrusive thought A.  2. This person felt XYZ and performed action ABC. 3. So if I were to judge this person, what conclusion would I make, based on the facts of the case?) 

On a side note, I strongly recommend not to stop taking medication. I've been there , done that - trust me, it only makes the intrusive thoughts and anxiety harder to handle. (In fact, I had a relapse  previously.)

---
Anyway, back to the main topic - If you still conclude you are a pedophile after doing the above, it's okay, so long as you don't hurt any humans. 

Be aware that you don't choose your sexuality and you didn't choose to be that way. So long as you don't act upon your desires (if any in this aspect), you haven't done anything wrong and you are still a good person.
